items.titleEn: The Bridge That Named a City
items.bodyEn: Most big rivers on the Tōkaidō had no bridge; you waded or took a ferry. The Toyokawa at Yoshida was an exception, spanned by a long bridge the shogunate kept in repair. Hiroshige shows it behind Yoshida Castle, where a workman on scaffolding waves at the view. In 1869 the castle town took the bridge's name and became Toyohashi.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō 'Yoshida: Toyokawa Bridge'; 1869 renaming of Yoshida domain

items.titleEn: No Difference, So It Must Be
items.bodyEn: 違 joins the road radical 辶 to 韋, an old picture of feet circling a walled place in opposite directions. The Shuowen glosses it 離也, 'to part ways'. Going the other way gives 違う (differ) and 間違い (mistake). 〜に違いない, this station's pattern, means literally 'there is no divergence from it' — hence 'it must be so'.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi, entry 違 (離也。从辵韋聲); standard kanji dictionaries on 韋

items.titleEn: A マンション Is Not a Mansion
items.bodyEn: Katakana words keep an English look but set their own meanings. マンション is a concrete apartment block or one unit in it, not a mansion; アパート is a smaller, lighter building. サービス often means 'on the house'. Learn loanwords as Japanese words: the dictionary that counts is the Japanese one, so J-J definitions begin here.

'Tap even a stone bridge before you cross it' — check what is already safe. On a road where bridges were wooden, rare and often washed away, a stone one was the picture of solidity, so testing it is caution carried to excess. Said of careful people with admiration or gentle teasing. Its cousin: 念には念を入れる, to make doubly sure.
